section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: Determinants as Area
section_1.content: Briefly define the determinant of a 2x2 matrix as the 'signed area' of a parallelogram formed by the column vectors (a, b) and (c, d). Visualize this as a transformation of the unit square.
section_1.example: Visualize the vector pair [2, 0] and [0, 2] creating a square with area 4. The determinant is 4.

section_2.title: Framing the System as Column Vectors
section_2.content: Introduce the system Ax = b as a linear combination of columns: x(col1) + y(col2) = b. Explain that we are looking for the 'weights' x and y that scale the columns to reach the target point b.
section_2.example: A delivery drone (target b) is powered by two propellers with thrust vectors v1 and v2. We need to find the power settings x and y to reach the target.

section_3.title: Geometric Substitution (The 'Area-Ratio' Logic)
section_3.content: Explain Cramer's Rule geometrically: Replacing a column vector with b creates a new parallelogram. The ratio of the area of this new parallelogram to the original determines the scalar needed to reach the target.
section_3.example: Show an animation where replacing the 'x-axis' vector with the target vector 'b' creates a new shape. The ratio of its area to the original area gives the x-coordinate.

section_4.title: Putting it Together: The Visual Formula
section_4.content: Formalize the rule: x = Det(A_x) / Det(A). Explain that because areas scale linearly, the ratio of areas perfectly isolates the scalar we are searching for.
section_4.example: Calculate x for a system: 2x + 1y = 5, 1x + 2y = 4. Use the visual area boxes to show how the division of the 'new' parallelogram area by the 'original' area results in x=2, y=1.

section_5.title: Summary & Intuition Check
section_5.content: Conclude by highlighting why this is powerful: It turns a 'searching for unknowns' problem into an 'area comparison' problem. Note the limitation: This only works when the determinant is non-zero (i.e., vectors aren't collinear).
section_5.example: An animation of two vectors collapsing into a single line (determinant 0) to show why Cramer's rule fails when the 'parallelogram' has no area.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 1.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.5 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
